name: Duplex / triplex / fourplex
summary: Small 2–4 unit 'missing middle' buildings, usually wood frame on a single lot. Per-SF cost runs a little above townhomes: small project scale, repeated kitchens and baths in smaller units, and fire separations. Triplexes and fourplexes often trigger commercial-code (IBC R-2) sprinklers and separate utility services. Direct cost data is thin. The only primary cost points are Washington permit valuations; national values are derived from townhome and single-family data. Treat as a derived estimate.

typicalSize.method: Units per project: one building of 2–4 units, or two fourplexes on a double lot. Census reports 20% of multifamily buildings completed in 2025 had two units (e3).

sfPerPrimaryUnit.method: Gross building SF per unit. Census 2025 multifamily units completed: median 1,000 SF built-for-rent, 1,170 SF built-for-sale (e3, net unit area). ~5–10% added for stairs and walls in small buildings. Side-by-side duplexes run larger (1,300–1,800 SF).

primaryUnitsPerAcre.method: A duplex on a 6,000 SF lot ≈ 14.5 du/net acre; a fourplex on a 7,000 SF lot ≈ 25 du/acre. Judgment from typical missing-middle zoning lot sizes.

parkingPerPrimaryUnit.method: Recent missing-middle reforms often allow 0–1 space per unit; suburban codes require 1.5–2. Judgment.

perPrimaryUnit.method: = perSF × sfPerPrimaryUnit: mid $160 × 1,150 ≈ $185k; low $120 × 900 ≈ $110k; high $210 × 1,400 ≈ $295k. WA cross-check: Snohomish County 2025 permit valuations $358.5k/unit for duplexes (e1) and $272k/unit for 3–4 unit buildings (e2), Seattle metro, with unit sizes not stated. Dividing by an assumed ~1.2 Seattle-to-national factor gives ~$300k and ~$227k. Those sit in the upper half of the range, consistent with larger WA units.

perSF.method: Derived from the townhomes per-SF range (115/150/200, from Census attached-home prices and WA permit valuations) +~7%. The premium is a judgment for small-builder scale, higher kitchen/bath density in ~1,000 SF units, and rated floor/ceiling separations in stacked units. No national per-SF source for 2–4 unit buildings was found.

scope.notes: Contractor price incl. GC general conditions and OH&P for the building plus on-lot work (driveway/parking pad, walks, laterals, landscaping). Excludes land, demolition of an existing house, off-site improvements, impact/tap fees and separate meter fees, A&E, financing and FF&E.

qualityTiers.method: Economy = low/mid of the per-SF range (120/160 = 0.75), rounded up slightly. Premium and luxury follow the townhome tiers. Judgment.

systemSplit.method: Derived from the single-family split (NAHB 2024 Table 1 mapped to CSI). Adjustments, all judgment: Div 01 up (small-project GC overhead); 21 added (13D/13R sprinklers for 3–4 unit buildings); 22, 11 and 12 up (one kitchen and 1–2 baths per ~1,100 SF); 09 up (rated assemblies); 31 and 32 down (single small lot); 33 for separate water/sewer services.

lineItems.name: Fire sprinkler system (NFPA 13D/13R) — triplex/fourplex

cost.method: Judgment: Div 21 ≈ 1.5–2.5% of a $160/SF building. A new water service upsize may add more. Verify locally.

lineItems.notes: Triplexes and fourplexes fall under the IBC (R-2) and usually require sprinklers; duplexes under the IRC often do not.

lineItems.name: Separate water/electric/gas services and meters per unit

cost.method: Judgment for on-lot laterals, meter banks and service equipment per unit; utility connection/tap fees are excluded (soft costs). The ADU evidence (adu.json) shows single new meters can cost $10k–30k in some cities.

lineItems.name: Demolition of existing single-family house (infill lot)

cost.method: Judgment for a 1,200–2,000 SF wood house incl. utility disconnects and hauling. Asbestos abatement is extra.

lineItems.notes: Most missing-middle projects replace an existing house.

pctOfHard.method: Starts from the single-family NAHB structure (fees ≈ 5%, A&E ≈ 1.6% of direct cost). A&E raised to ~5–7% (custom small-building design, structural/energy engineering for R-2) and per-unit impact and utility fees raised. No developer marketing overhead at this scale. Mid ≈ 21%. Judgment.

softCosts.notes: Impact and connection fees are often assessed per dwelling unit and can dominate on small projects.

hard.method: Judgment: infill sites carry unknowns (old utilities, soils).

perPrimaryUnit.method: Low hard $110k × 1.12 ≈ $125k; high $295k × 1.35 ≈ $400k, plus headroom for coastal metros. Excludes land.

source.title: Issued Residential Building Permits — September 2025, Unincorporated Snohomish County
source.publisher: Snohomish County Planning and Development Services

evidence.scopeNotes: Researcher computed $1,434,025 / 4 units = $358,506/unit. Permit valuation (building value), unit sizes not stated. Small sample (2 buildings).

source.title: Highlights of Annual 2025 Characteristics of New Housing

evidence.quote: The median size of multifamily units completed that were built for rent was 1,000 square feet
evidence.scopeNotes: Built-for-sale multifamily median was 1,170 SF. The same page reports 20% of multifamily buildings completed in 2025 had two units. All multifamily, not only 2–4 unit buildings.

openQuestions: No national hard-cost source for 2–4 unit buildings. Missing-middle feasibility studies (e.g., Portland Residential Infill Project, California SB 9 analyses, Opticos) or RSMeans R-2/R-3 square-foot models would replace the derived per-SF.
Permit valuations (Snohomish) lack unit SF, so per-SF could not be computed.
